neurological_exam.additional: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: The cognitive-behavioral syndrome is being attributed to Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) or PD-MCI. HOWEVER: (1) The BEHAVIORAL profile is wrong for PDD — PDD causes visuospatial impairment, hallucinations, attention fluctuation, NOT the disinhibition/perseveration/social cognition loss pattern; (2) PDD onset occurs LATE in PD (typically >10 years, mean 10 years after motor onset) — this patient has only 4-year PD history; (3) DATscan will show asymmetric dopaminergic deficit consistent with PD, but cannot distinguish PDD from bvFTD with PD; (4) The behavioral syndrome preceded or occurred simultaneously with the PD diagnosis. This may represent a Parkinson-FTD overlap syndrome.

patient.chief_complaint: Cognitive and behavioral decline attributed to Parkinson's disease — 20 months progressive; behavioral features discordant with PDD pattern
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N is a 52-year-old investment banker, terminated 20 months ago, who has been followed by a general neurologist for Parkinson's disease (diagnosed 4 years ago, mild right-sided onset). He was referred to the cognitive neurology clinic after his primary neurologist expressed concern that the cognitive and behavioral changes 'don't fit the expected pattern for PD-MCI.' He was initially diagnosed with PD-MCI by a prior neurologist 2 years ago and has been managed with carbidopa/levodopa with good motor response. His wife of 2 years — he married her during the period of behavioral changes — is the primary informant. She describes behaviors that preceded their marriage and were not apparent to her at the time: he made several large, impulsive financial decisions shortly before they met that his family has since described to her as completely uncharacteristic. He spent $180,000 on a collection of vintage motorcycles within 6 months, despite having no prior interest in motorcycles. He was terminated from his bank position for 'performance and conduct issues' — he had made unauthorized client fund transfers and made multiple sexually inappropriate comments to a junior colleague. He denied all of these events and filed an unsuccessful wrongful termination suit. He is now in a persistent legal battle over a disputed real estate transaction he initiated. At home, he has a highly rigid routine — he eats the same three items for breakfast in identical order each day and becomes enraged if the sequence is altered. He has stopped reading financial news, which was his lifelong obsession. He has no insight into any of these behaviors. Importantly, his motor PD symptoms have remained mild and respond well to levodopa. His father has Parkinson's disease and advanced cognitive impairment (in a memory care facility at age 82). The key diagnostic question: is this Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) presenting early due to a genetic PD variant? Or is this behavioral variant FTD that happens to coexist with (or cause) Parkinson-like features? The behavioral profile — disinhibition, perseveration, loss of empathy, impulsive financial decisions — is FTD, not PDD.

results.title: C9orf72 expansion in frontotemporal dementia with and without parkinsonism
A hexanucleotide repeat in C9ORF72 is the cause of chromosome 9p21-linked ALS-FTD

output.summary: C9orf72 expansion can produce a broad phenotypic spectrum including: (1) bvFTD alone; (2) ALS alone; (3) combined FTD-ALS; (4) FTD with Parkinsonism; (5) Parkinson's disease alone (rare). When FTD and Parkinsonism coexist in a C9orf72 carrier, the key FDG-PET discriminating feature is critical: PDD/DLB shows posterior cortex (parietal, occipital) hypometabolism, while C9orf72-FTD with Parkinsonism shows FRONTAL hypometabolism with preserved posterior cortex. DaTscan is abnormal in both PDD and FTD-Parkinsonism — it confirms dopaminergic deficit but cannot distinguish the cognitive syndrome type. FDG-PET is the critical differentiating test.

output.proposed: Ongoing management of bvFTD-C9orf72 with coexistent Parkinsonism — levodopa continuation
interactions: Levodopa + sertraline: minimal interaction; sertraline is safe with levodopa in PD
contraindications: Cholinesterase inhibitors — CONTRAINDICATED in FTD even in PD patient; do not prescribe donepezil for this patient
warnings: Continue levodopa for Parkinsonian motor symptoms — it treats the PD motor component but will NOT improve bvFTD behavioral symptoms
Sertraline 100 mg may modestly help bvFTD behavioral symptoms (disinhibition) — continue
Monitor for ALS features annually (EMG) — C9orf72 ALS risk
Genetic counseling for family — 50% inheritance risk for children

differential.key_features: FDG-PET shows FRONTAL hypometabolism with preserved posterior and occipital cortex — opposite of PDD/DLB pattern (posterior hypometabolism); behavioral profile (disinhibition, perseveration, social cognition loss) is FTD, not PDD (which causes visuospatial impairment, hallucinations, attention fluctuation); PD motor onset only 4 years ago (PDD typically >10 years post-motor onset)
FDG-PET preserved occipital cortex (DLB signature is occipital hypometabolism); amyloid PET negative; no fluctuating cognition; no visual hallucinations; no REM sleep behavior disorder history

No midbrain atrophy (hummingbird sign absent); no falls; no supranuclear gaze palsy; no axial rigidity predominance; frontal behavioral syndrome rather than PSP-Richardson (which has apathy, not disinhibition)
Amyloid PET negative; frontal FDG-PET without posterior cingulate sign; behavioral disinhibition/perseveration is FTD not AD

critical_actions: FDG-PET is the key discriminating test between PDD and bvFTD-with-Parkinsonism: PDD/DLB = posterior hypometabolism; bvFTD = frontal hypometabolism with preserved posterior cortex; DaTscan alone CANNOT make this distinction
Do NOT prescribe cholinesterase inhibitors even though patient has PD — FTD component is primary cognitive diagnosis and cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated in FTD
C9orf72 genetic testing is essential in FTD-Parkinsonism overlap — it explains both the FTD and the Parkinson-like features
contraindicated_actions: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) — contraindicated despite PD diagnosis; FTD is the primary cognitive syndrome
Attributing behavioral syndrome entirely to PD without FDG-PET characterization of the metabolic pattern
key_reasoning_points: DaTscan confirms dopaminergic deficit (PD) but is BLIND to the cognitive syndrome type — PDD and bvFTD with Parkinsonism both have abnormal DaTscans; FDG-PET is the discriminating test

FDG-PET posterior cortex preservation is the KEY: PDD and DLB always show posterior (parietal and/or occipital) hypometabolism; bvFTD shows frontal hypometabolism with PRESERVED posterior cortex — these are opposites

Behavioral profile is the second key discriminating feature: PDD causes visuospatial impairment, fluctuating cognition, hallucinations; bvFTD causes disinhibition, perseveration, social cognition loss — these syndromes are clinically distinct
C9orf72 expansion can cause FTD-Parkinsonism overlap syndrome — it causes both the behavioral FTD and contributes to the Parkinsonian motor features via TDP-43 pathology in the substantia nigra

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle bvFTD — C9orf72 with Parkinsonism, masquerading as PDD. Key teaching: DaTscan cannot distinguish PDD from FTD-Parkinsonism; FDG-PET posterior preservation rules out PDD; cholinesterase inhibitors contraindicated even in PD patient when FTD is primary diagnosis.
